agenda_text:
October 6, 2025

Ms. Jessie Fan, ENV SP
Kimley-Horn
660 South Figueroa Street, Suite 2050
Los Angeles, California 90017

Subject:  Additional Response to Comments for the Rubio Village Mixed-Use Project
  IS/MND 201-205 South San Gabriel Boulevard, San Gabriel, Los Angeles
  County, California
Ms. Fan:
Rocks Biological Consulting (RBC) is providing a response to supplemental comments received on
October 1, 2025, for the 2.9-acre mixed-use residential and commercial Rubio Village Project
(project) in City of San Gabriel (City), Los Angeles County, California.

Initial CEQA Comment Letters
An Initial Study/Mitigated Negative Declaration (IS/MND) was previously prepared for the project in
August 2023. In their September 2023 comment letter on the City’s 2023 Draft IS/MND for the
project and additional December 2023 response, Supporter’s Alliance for Environmental
Responsibility (SAFER) indicated that a project site visit was conducted by an independent
biological expert and concerns were raised regarding project impacts to special-status species.
SAFER’s biologist Dr. Shawn Smallwood identified common, native avian species utilizing the
proposed project site including the following: black phoebe, Anna’s hummingbird, house finch,
northern mockingbird, mourning dove, band-tailed pigeon, American crow, common raven,
California towhee, American kestrel, and red-winged blackbird. Two species that are on the
USFWS BCC list, Allen’s hummingbird and western gull, were also identified by Dr. Smallwood on
the project site. Introduced species that are not native to California, red-crowned parrot, rock
pigeon, European starling, and Eurasian collared dove, were also observed by Dr. Smallwood. It
was subsequently determined that a Biological Resources Report prepared by qualified biologists
was warranted for the city to further evaluate the project impacts under the California
Environmental Quality Act (CEQA).
Subsequent Biological Studies
RBC qualified biologists conducted a field survey of the project site on June 5, 2025, and prepared
a Biological Resources Assessment Report (Biological Report) dated August 27, 2025, in support
of the City’s additional CEQA documentation. Several of the same avian species as documented
by Dr. Smallwood were also documented during RBC’s June 2025 site visit as reported in the
August 2025 Biological Report. However, based on the field reconnaissance survey, database and
literature searches, and overall assessment, it was concluded that the proposed project area
development is not likely to significantly impact sensitive biological resources if the mitigation
measure recommended to avoid impacts to nesting birds is incorporated. No sensitive wildlife or

plant species were found during the site survey with the exception of a non-listed nesting raptor
located approximately 430 feet from the site (outside of the Survey Area).
The site was found to contain potentially suitable habitat for common nesting passerines and
landbirds. These species could occasionally occur onsite and on adjacent properties. RBC
recommended implementing mitigation measure BIO-1 for compliance with MBTA and CFGC
requirements, which would detect and provide protection for nesting bird species should they
become established onsite or adjacent. Due to the surrounding high density urban setting,
historical developed use of the site, and resulting disturbed land cover, it was concluded that the
project would not have a substantial adverse effect on sensitive natural communities or wildlife
movement in the area.
Additional Comment Letters and Response
Primary points raised in the additional comment letter provided by SAFER on October 1, 2025, are
similar to those previously provided. Additionally, Dr. Smallwood reported results of subsequent
site surveys that he conducted in April 2025. The October 2025 comment letter asserts that the
Project may have ‘Significant Unmitigated Impacts on Biological Resources’ and that preparation
of an Environmental Impact Report is warranted. A breakdown of the key points of the comment
letter and associated responses are as follows:
  A. Comment: Project Site provides habitat for special-status species. Dr. Smallwood
  and Noriko Smallwood observed BCC birds (Allen’s hummingbird, western gull), non-
  listed raptor species (American kestrel, red-shouldered hawk, and turkey vulture), and
  silver-haired bat (IUCN-LC) on site or flying over the site and thus concludes the site
  provides foraging habitat for these species and nesting habitat for Allen’s
  hummingbirds. Comment claims the Biological Report does not adequately identify the
  potential for these species to utilize the site.
  Response: The Biological Report acknowledges the potential presence of these avian
  species on site which do occur in urbanized and residential settings. An evaluation of
  the potential for special-status bats is provided in Appendix A and on pages 9-10.
  Occurrences of special-status bats in the region, i.e. those that are considered state
  Species of Concern, are more than 100 years old and assumed to be prior to
  surrounding urbanization. Trees on site are not suitable for bat roosting which does not
  seem to be refuted by Dr. Smallwood. Rubio Wash is identified as potential foraging
  habitat for common bats. Silver-haired bat as identified by Dr. Smallwood on site is not
  considered a state Species of Concern and falls into the category of ‘Least Concern’
  from the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). It may forage in Rubio
  Wash along with other common bat species as was stated in the Biological Report and
  analyzed accordingly.
  B. Comment: Substantial evidence the Project may result in significant impacts on
  special-status species. Due to:

  2

  October 6, 2025

1. Habitat Loss - Comment: Area around the site has experienced severe habitat
  fragmentation and this is one of the last patches of naturally-covered open
  space in the region. Rubio Wash attracts wildlife including silver-haired bats and
  the BCC and raptor species observed would lose foraging habitat with project
  construction. Allen’s hummingbird (BCC) may lose nesting habitat.
  Response: The site is not considered ‘naturally-covered’ from a habitat or
  vegetation community standpoint. It was previously developed with demolition
  of buildings and associated infrastructure occurring in the last 10 years.
  Recruitment of vegetation did occur as the site was left undeveloped in
  intervening years. Land cover of the site is currently categorized as disturbed
  with a prevalence of non-native vegetation as is common in disturbed settings.
  This is reflected by results of the biological survey as reported in Appendix C of
  the biological report which includes an inventory of plant species documented
  on site. Native soils are absent as reflected by the site soils maps (Figure 3 of
  the biological report) having been previously removed and replaced with
  imported fill. No natural, native vegetation communities are present as a result.
  Rubio Wash would not be altered from its current state.
  Significance criteria defined by CEQA guidelines and sensitivity under CEQA is
  more inclusive than federal and State laws regulating biological resources.
  Resources without a formal, statute binding protection status do receive
  consideration under CEQA. ‘Watchlist’ species, ‘species of concern’, ‘species
  of conservation concern’, and other species tracked at population levels,
  identified by State, regional, and local agencies, as well as conservation
  organizations, receive consideration in the CEQA review process.
  BCC such as western gull and Allen’s hummingbird have some level of
  sensitivity, and their populations are being tracked by the USFWS. As
  discussed in Section 4.3 of the Biological Report, BCC individuals Allen’s
  hummingbird and western gull as observed by SAFER’s biologist, may use the
  site. Birds of prey, such as the American kestrels, may forage but are not
  expected to nest on the project site due to a lack of suitable nest habitat. With
  implementation of MM-BIO-1, there would be no direct loss of individual BCC or
  raptors as required by the MBTA and CFGC. The IS/MND analysis and MM-
  BIO-1 satisfies the mitigation standard for BCC and birds of prey under CEQA
  as these species are afforded no formal protection other than the MBTA and
  CFGC. Additionally, BCC do not meet the definition of “rare” under CEQA as
  clarified in Nassiri v. City of Lafayette. In a recent California First District Court of
  Appeal (Nassiri v. City of Lafayette, et al. (2024) 103 Cal.App.5th 910), the court
  clarified the definition of “rare” species as applied under CEQA and specifically
  to BCC. The court stated that a federal or State agency’s mere designation of a
  species as a “species of conservation concern” is not equivalent to being

  3
   Rubio Village Project
  October 6, 2025
  Page 4 of 6

  deemed “rare”. So long as a lead agency has evidence that a species is not
  listed under the CESA or ESA, is not rare or unique in the area, or imminently at
  risk of endangerment, it is not considered “rare” under the CEQA Guidelines.
  As the Lead Agency under CEQA, the city, with input from technical specialists
  and responsible agencies, may determine the significance of potential impacts
  to special-status species that are not formally listed, proposed for listing, or
  defined as “rare”. CDFW, USFWS, and other State agencies responsible for
  regulating biological resources have not raised concerns regarding the
  biological impacts associated with this project. Accordingly, the site’s value to
  common wildlife species, non-listed raptors, and the observation of two BCC
  birds, does not reach a level of significance as defined under CEQA that
  warrants the more detailed environmental analysis provided by an EIR as is
  called for by SAFER in their comment letters. The city has completed an
  adequate biological analysis and prescribed mitigation for sensitive resources
  on site that is within industry standards and in line with CEQA precedent for infill
  projects in urbanized settings. The IS/MND prepared for the project
  appropriately identifies these potential impacts to biological resources and
  prescribes mitigation measures to reduce impacts to a less than significant level
  via avian pre-construction surveys (BIO-1). This is a precedented industry
  standard and typical mitigation measure for infill sites such as this project.
  Therefore, the methodologies and analysis described in the IS/MND, as well as
  the supplemental information from the biological report, substantiate that the
  project, with implementation of MM-BIO-1, would have a less than significant
  impact on special-status species, and additional CEQA analysis is not
  warranted.
2. Interference with Wildlife Movement – Comment: Site is critically important to
  wildlife movement and project may interfere substantially with wildlife
  movement. Rubio Wash is a feature likely to be followed by wildlife moving
  through the region.
  Response: Rubio Wash will remain in its current state with construction of the
  project, continuing to provide local wildlife movement opportunities. As
  described in the Biological Report, the project is located in an highly urbanized
  area of Los Angeles County. The site is not within any mapped or known
  California Essential Habitat Connectivity area. It is surrounded by high density
  residential and commercial development. The site is also bounded by roadways
  including the highly trafficked San Gabriel Boulevard to the east. The project site
  is isolated from open spaces and natural habitats by the surrounding urban
  development. The closest ‘green spaces’ consist of actively managed golf
  courses to the north and southwest. No other parks or recreational open

  4
   Rubio Village Project
  October 6, 2025
  Page 5 of 6

  spaces lie in the vicinity. Common avian species do utilize the vegetation in the
  area. However, given the disturbed setting, limited quality of wildlife habitat on
  site, and barriers to dispersal in the form of roads and buildings surrounding the
  site, it provides very limited opportunities for wildlife movement and there is no
  connectivity to more natural habitats in the region. Whittier Narrows Recreation
  Area, approximately five miles away, is the closest natural habitat. Wildlife
  movement through the site would be characterized as local, by urban adapted
  species use and not associated with an important regional movement corridor
  for sensitive or rare species occurring in natural or native habitat types.
  Local wildlife movements by common urban adapted species such as coyotes
  and raccoons may occur through the site and along Rubio Wash which
  provides some connectivity offsite, although no vegetation or cover is present
  as the channel is entirely concrete lined. Rubio Wash turns into an underground
  pipeline as it leaves the site to the north. Thus, connectivity to other daylighted
  portions of the channel would be limited to areas south of the site. The
  constructed project will maintain Rubio Wash in its current state with exception
  of free spanning pedestrian bridges. Disturbance during construction of the
  project may temporarily affect localized wildlife movement along the channel.
  However, once construction is complete, opportunities for wildlife movement
  would resume and potentially be enhanced through creation of landscaped
  open spaces next to Rubio Wash. For these reasons which were described in
  the IS/MND and Biological Report, the project would have a less than significant
  impact on local wildlife movement corridors and no impact on regional wildlife
  movement.
  3. Bird-Window Collisions – Comment: Construction of 70 foot tall buildings may
  result in significant bird-window strikes and projects up to 475 annual bird
  deaths per year.
  Response: The studies that were considered in the comment that led to the
  commenter’s predictions are based on multiple sources across the United
  States, the majority of which are in environments and settings that are not
  representative of an urban environment like the project site, where there is less
  likelihood for special-status avian species to be present. Summarizing data from
  multiple articles without taking into account the actual level of avian
  observations, and the preexisting urbanized landscape does not conclusively
  yield an accurate average collision rate. Therefore, the estimation of 475 annual
  bird deaths per year would not be accurate for this project site.
Conclusion
As concluded in the Biological Report prepared by RBC dated August 27, 2025, while several of
the same avian species as documented by SAFER were also documented by RBC, development

  5
   Rubio Village Project
  October 6, 2025
  Page 6 of 6

of the project would not result in significant impacts to sensitive biological resources with
incorporation of mitigation measure BIO-1. SAFER’s observations do not equate to the Project Site
supporting significantly important habitat for rare species under CEQA. Therefore, SAFER has not
presented substantial evidence that the Project would result in significant impacts on special-status
species such that an EIR would be required.
Thank you very much for the opportunity to respond to these comments. Please don’t hesitate to
contact me with any questions or concerns at (858) 243-1505.

Sincerely,

Angie Harbin
Principal Biologist
